chapter.title: Four Hundred Rooms
chapter.sub: A new job, four hundred rooms and a wall of green tiles — while twenty-two rooms record silence.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 5 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT · CASE-025  Countdown · Maya, Nadia and Wes · Level L4 · Intermediate support  A new job, four hundred rooms, and a wall of green tiles. Twenty-two of those rooms have recorded silence for three days — and the dashboard never noticed.  ⚑ RV-121: figures illustrative. RV-122: generic systems. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Four Hundred Rooms
items.stakes: Twenty-two rooms have recorded silence for three days, and the wall of green tiles says everything is fine. The students who watch recordings — because of jobs, kids, illness — are the ones it hurts.
items.reward: Every room recording with sound, proven. A dashboard that measures what students get. Nadia's trust in her new engineer.

objectives.text: Find out why the wall stayed green
Give the recording its sound back
Prove it in rooms you'll never visit
Look closer: two things about Kai

items.rumor: Four hundred rooms. You'll see forty. The wall shows you the rest — if it's watching the right thing.

items.sub: Kestrel Valley · the morning after the crest

items.alt: Flashback: master control at Kestrel Valley Media, dawn after the flood crest. Maya on the phone; Tess watching her from the desk.

bubbles.text: Tell them no, Priya. I'm not going to be the one who takes master control out of the valley.
…Then who's going to be here when it goes?

items.alt: Spring. The Brackenmoor University quad: two brick buildings, a path, a campus information kiosk. Maya walks in with a new lanyard.
narration: Brackenmoor University & Teaching Hospital. Four hundred teaching rooms. Sixty clinical rooms. One arena. Day one.
items.caption: She took a job where the rooms don't know her name yet.

items.alt: The AV operations office: a wall of 400 green room tiles. Nadia, the AV operations manager, points at it; Maya takes it in.

bubbles.text: That's the campus. Green means fine.

items.caption: Remember her question.

lines.text: Four hundred teaching rooms. Sixty clinical. One arena. You'll stand in maybe forty this year.
And the other three hundred and sixty?
You'll know them through that wall. Or you won't.

items.alt: Wes, a student worker in a green hoodie and a crooked headset, arrives with two coffees and hands one to Maya.

bubbles.text: I'm Wes. I'm supposed to shadow you. I brought coffee in case you're mean.
I'm not mean. I ask a lot of questions.

items.prompt: (Wes, on his second shift, headset crooked) Do I call you Maya or, like, boss?

options.label: “Maya. And you're not shadowing me — you're doing it. I'll ask why.”
“Boss works.”
options.reply: Cool. Boss. I'll just… watch, then.

options.label: “Ask me that after you've fixed something.”

items.alt: A ticket on a phone screen, submitted at 2:14 a.m. by a student named Kai: all his Engineering lectures since Saturday have no sound.
items.caption: Tuesday, 10:48. The first ticket about it. Three days in.

items.title: Submitted 2:14 a.m.
items.body: *All my Engineering lectures since Saturday have no sound. I work nights at the depot and I watch them after. I thought it was my laptop, so I bought headphones. It isn't my laptop.* He bought headphones before he filed a ticket.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #42 · AVERY'S LENS  Measure the outcome, not the heartbeat  A dashboard should turn red when the user's result fails — not only when a device stops answering.  Twenty-two capture appliances answered every ping for three days while every recording they made was silent.

items.alt: The dashboard zoomed to the Engineering building: 22 of 22 capture appliances online, ping OK, disk OK. Wes throws his hands up.

items.prompt: 10:52. ENG-214's next lecture starts at 11:00 and it will record silent too. What do you do in eight minutes?
items.happening: Dashboard green. Kai's ticket open. ENG-214 at 11:00.
items.risk: Another silent lecture — and the evidence of why.
timeout: 11:00 arrives. ENG-214 records another silent lecture.
Eight minutes was enough for one room — if someone had started.

hints.text: What is the appliance actually listening to?

options.label: Reboot all 22 capture appliances remotely
options.result: Eight minutes of reboots. At 11:00 they're still recording silence — and Saturday's status logs are gone.
options.consequence: A reboot doesn't change a setting; it erases the evidence.

options.label: Read ENG-214's capture status, fix that one room, and make a test recording before 11:00
options.result: INPUT: USB · level −∞. Switched to LINE. A 30-second test recording: Wes counting to ten.
options.consequence: One reversible change, one room, with proof on the way.

options.label: Ask the vendor to roll everything back now
options.result: Their change desk opens at noon. The 11:00 lecture records silent.

options.label: Tell the lecturer to record on her phone
options.result: She does. It sounds like a phone in a pocket.
options.consequence: A workaround for one room, one hour.

items.alt: The capture appliance's status page: online, disk OK — input USB, level minus infinity, firmware updated Saturday 2 a.m. Maya points at the input line.
items.caption: Online. Healthy. Listening to nothing.

items.title: Green all along.
items.body: The dashboard never checked sound. Its tiles turn green when an appliance answers the network and its disk has space. Twenty-two appliances answered faithfully for three days while every recording they made was silent. A heartbeat, not an outcome.
items.label: Test: what does this rule out as proof?

items.alt: Maya explains to Wes at the dashboard.

bubbles.text: A heartbeat says 'I'm here'. An outcome says 'you got what you came for'. The wall only knows heartbeats.
So we need a tile that turns red when a lecture is silent.

lines.text: It's all green. Every tile. How is it all green?
Because it's asking the wrong question. 'Are you there?' Not 'did anyone hear the lecture?'

items.alt: System View of ENG-214: mics and DSP fine; loudspeakers fine; the capture appliance listening to its empty USB input; the portal silent. Below: the dashboard's heartbeat says online; the student's outcome is silence.
items.caption: The room hears everything. The recording hears nothing.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Wes beside a board. Percent is part over whole, times a hundred. Part: the rooms that failed. Whole: every room we have. Twenty-two over four hundred… five and a half percent. Then the time budget: count times time each. Twenty-two rooms, six minutes to prove each. Say it before you promise it.

bubbles.text: Percent is part over whole, times a hundred. Part: the rooms that failed. Whole: every room we have.
Twenty-two over four hundred… five and a half percent.
Then the time budget: count times time each. Twenty-two rooms, six minutes to prove each. Say it before you promise it.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Outcome check   Heartbeat check   Update ring   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Percentage  % = part ÷ whole × 100   part  the piece you are measuring  whole  everything it is part of     ƒ FORMULA · Time budget  T = Σ (count × time each)   count  how many of each task  time each  minutes or seconds per task — keep units the same

items.label: **Fix it:** give the recording its sound back.

items.alt: The vendor's change record: ring 1 was defined as ENG*, intended as four pilot rooms, and it matched 22. The new firmware changed the default input from LINE to USB.
items.caption: A pilot of four became a building of twenty-two.

items.title: ENG-B12 · basement lab
items.body: The last room the wildcard caught is ENG-B12, the basement lab. Kai's section meets there on Tuesdays. Three lab lectures, silent. Maya writes his name on a sticky note and puts it on her monitor.

items.title: ENG* matched everything — including ENG-B12.
items.body: The wildcard caught every Engineering room, down to ENG-B12 in the basement — the lab room where Kai's section meets on Tuesdays. The student who reported it at 2 a.m. had already missed three lab lectures.
items.label: Test: who does this change things for?
**Learn it now:** monitoring outcomes at scale.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · tap a plate to open it full size     Sound that brings people in     What the room is telling you     The five fundamentals of sound

items.prompt: ENG-214 is fixed. Twenty-one rooms to go, and you'll never stand in most of them. How do you prove each one?
known: ◉ One room proven by test recording
unknown: Whether each room took the profile
items.risk: Declaring 21 rooms fixed on the wall's word.
timeout: Wes pushes the profile and everyone watches the tiles stay green.
Green told you nothing on Saturday either.

hints.text: Which path does Kai use to hear a lecture?

options.label: When each tile turns green
options.result: Every tile was green while they recorded silence.
options.consequence: The wall was never measuring this.

options.label: A 30-second test recording in each room, played back from the student portal
options.result: Twenty-one test recordings. Wes plays each one back on a student account. Every one has sound.
options.consequence: Proof on the path the students use.

options.label: Ask lecturers to email if it's still silent
options.result: They don't know it's silent — they never watch their own recordings.
options.consequence: The people who'd notice aren't the ones you asked.

options.label: Walk to all 21 rooms
options.consequence: It works for 21. It won't work for 400.

items.title: The first recorded voice to play back
items.body: In December 1877 Thomas Edison recited “Mary had a little lamb” into a machine that cut the sound into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder — and heard it played back. The phonograph was astonishing because it proved what it had captured by giving it back. Every test recording since has done the same job: don't trust the machine, listen to what it kept.

items.alt: Wes on a student account plays back test recordings one after another; each one has his own voice counting to ten. Maya checks them off a list.

bubbles.text: Twenty-one rooms of me counting to ten. I sound terrible.

items.prompt: Friday. What changes so the next silence isn't found by a student at 2 a.m.?
timeout: The week ends. Nobody changes the wall.
Fixing the room without fixing the wall leaves the next room to a student.

hints.text: What would have turned a tile red on Saturday?

options.label: An audio-level check on every capture appliance, and a change request: rings use explicit room lists
options.result: Silent recordings now turn a tile red in ten minutes. The vendor agrees in writing.
options.consequence: The dashboard measures the outcome; the process can't grow a pilot into a building.

options.label: Block all vendor updates
options.result: Next month's security fix doesn't install.
options.consequence: Trading one risk for a bigger one.
options.fail: Updates carry security fixes; control them, don't stop them.

options.label: Email the vendor's CEO
options.result: A satisfying email. Nothing changes on the wall.

options.label: Nothing — it's fixed
options.result: The next silent firmware lands in June.
options.consequence: The same wall, the same blind spot.
options.fail: A fix without a lesson repeats.

items.label: **First failure point:** where does the silence begin?
**Sequence:** prove a fix in rooms you'll never visit.

items.alt: System View after the fix: the capture appliance takes the DSP's line out; the portal has sound; the dashboard's new audio check is green because the outcome is good.
items.caption: Now green means the student heard the lecture.

lines.text: The logs were the only witness.

items.alt: A reply from Kai: the lectures have sound again; someone emailed him the lab notes; he returned the headphones.
items.caption: Behind every tile, a person you'll never meet.

items.alt: A hospital clinic room with a telehealth cart. Dr. Imogen Hale, the clinical simulation and telehealth lead, is on the phone.

bubbles.text: Maya? Imogen Hale, telehealth. Our carts freeze mid-consult. Only three rooms. Only weekday mornings. Patients are starting to hang up on their doctors.

items.caption: Next: *The Clinical Room.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A dashboard that checks whether devices answer can stay green while users fail. Measure the outcome — a recording with sound, a call that connects — and prove each fix on the path the user takes. Pilots are lists, not wildcards.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Kai bought headphones before he filed a ticket. What in your own systems makes people blame themselves first?
